slide.title: Where Does This Come From?
slide.body: Lineage graph: raw.repayments and raw.borrowers → staging boxes → fct_borrower_features, one path glowing teal. Small tag: Data Engineering for AI · Lesson 10.

scenes.on_screen_text: Where does this column come from?
scenes.voiceover: A data scientist asks: where does days since last come from, and does it include cancelled orders? If the answer lives only in your memory, every question interrupts you. And when you leave the team, the answer leaves with you.

slide.title: Documentation and Lineage
slide.body: Data Engineering for AI · Lesson 10 of 18

scenes.voiceover: Last time, we made models incremental. Today we make them understandable. In dbt, documentation lives next to the code. You add a description to each model and its important columns, in a YAML file. The same file will hold your tests later.

slide.title: Docs live next to the code
slide.body: Project folder: model .sql file and schema.yml side by side, both inside one Git commit box

scenes.voiceover: Because descriptions sit in the project, they are reviewed and versioned with the SQL. When the SQL changes, the description changes in the same step.

slide.title: Two commands
slide.body: dbt docs generate → catalogue of models, columns, types, descriptions. dbt docs serve → local web server, opens the site

scenes.voiceover: Two commands build a documentation site. The first, generate, reads the project and the database, and writes a catalogue of every model, column, type and description. The second, serve, starts a small local web server and opens the site in your browser.

slide.title: The lineage graph
slide.body: Boxes: sources (green) → staging models → marts, arrows labelled source() and ref(). Caption: built from your code, not drawn by hand

scenes.voiceover: The site includes the lineage graph. It shows every source and model as a box, with arrows that follow your source and ref calls. You did not draw this graph. dbt built it from your code. That is why using ref instead of written table names matters.

slide.title: Upstream and downstream
slide.body: Left arrow (upstream): wrong number → staging → source. Right arrow (downstream): source change → models → consumers affected.

scenes.voiceover: Lineage helps in two directions. Upstream: a number looks wrong, so you follow the arrows back to its staging model and source. Downstream: a source is about to change a column, so you follow the arrows forward to see every model and consumer it will affect.

slide.title: A good description says
slide.body: Grain: what one row means · Unit of each number · Time window of each feature · Traps, e.g. 'excludes cancelled orders'

scenes.voiceover: Good descriptions are short and specific. Say what one row means, the unit of each number, the time window of each feature, and anything a reader might misunderstand, such as excludes cancelled orders.

scenes.stock_query: reading a thick novel family tree
scenes.voiceover: Lineage is like the family tree at the front of a long novel. When a character appears in chapter twenty, you check the tree to see who their parents are. You do not reread the whole book.

scenes.stock_query: loan officer meeting small business owner
scenes.voiceover: Let's document a feature table. Priya is an analytics engineer at a microfinance lender in Pune, India. Loan officers ask many questions about her borrower feature table.

screen_steps: Type the fct_borrower_features model description from content.md
Highlight: 'One row per borrower per feature_date'
scenes.voiceover: She opens the schema file in the marts folder. For the model, she writes the grain, one row per borrower per feature date, the rule that it uses only repayments before that date, and what it is used for.

screen_steps: Type the borrower_id column description: internal ID from stg_borrowers, not a national ID
Type the late_payments_180d description from content.md
Add short descriptions for stg_repayments and stg_borrowers in models/staging/schema.yml
scenes.voiceover: Then she describes two columns. The borrower ID is an internal ID, not a national ID. And late payments in one hundred and eighty days counts instalments paid more than seven days late, in the hundred and eighty days before the feature date.

screen_steps: In the browser, open fct_borrower_features and show the descriptions and column types
scenes.voiceover: She runs generate, then serve, and the site opens in her browser. She opens the feature table, and shows the descriptions and column types.

screen_steps: Show raw.repayments → stg_repayments → fct_borrower_features and raw.borrowers → stg_borrowers → fct_borrower_features
Click stg_repayments and show its downstream models
scenes.on_screen_text: Upstream to source, downstream to impact
scenes.voiceover: Now the lineage graph. Two paths lead into the feature table: raw repayments through staging repayments, and raw borrowers through staging borrowers. She clicks staging repayments to show every model downstream of it.

slide.title: Answer in three sentences
slide.body: 1. Source: raw.repayments, nightly from the loan system. 2. stg_repayments: dates to DATE, test loans removed. 3. Feature: instalments > 7 days late in the 180 days before feature_date.

scenes.voiceover: Now Priya can answer in three sentences. The feature comes from raw repayments, received every night from the loan system. Staging converts the dates and removes test loans. The feature table counts instalments paid more than seven days late, in the hundred and eighty days before the feature date.

scenes.on_screen_text: Don't repeat the name. Explain it.
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is a description that only repeats the column name, such as late payments in one hundred and eighty days. That adds nothing. Answer what a new reader would ask: what counts as late, which dates are included, and where the value comes from. And update descriptions in the same change as the SQL, not once and then forget.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Descriptions in YAML, versioned with code. 2. dbt docs generate + serve → site and lineage. 3. Trace upstream; check impact downstream.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, dbt descriptions live in YAML next to the models, so documentation is versioned and reviewed with the code. Second, generate and serve build a documentation site, with a lineage graph created from source and ref. Third, lineage lets you trace a value upstream to its source, and see what a change affects downstream.

Now it is your turn. In the exercise, you will document three models and their key columns, generate the site, and use the lineage graph to explain where one feature column comes from, in three sentences. It takes about thirty minutes. Next week is about data quality, starting with: What Makes Data Bad?
